cases.title: The Florida Bar v. Catarcio
cases.citation: The Florida Bar v. Catarcio, 709 So. 2d 96 (Fla. 1998)

brief.facts: Catarcio, not a Florida Bar member, ran a legal-form preparation business and billed himself on his card as "Richard T. Catarcio, J.D." with the Scales of Justice. Robert Cooper came for help filing personal bankruptcy. Catarcio advised he was eligible and should file Chapter 7, told Cooper and his ex-wife Caron to file jointly (warning Caron the trustee would otherwise "come after" her), and told Cooper what to put in the petition. He decided where to file, checked the boxes for which statutory exemptions applied (Cooper did not understand them), advised what counted as joint property, selected the citations for the claimed exemptions, and explained the value of exempt property. He told Caron to sign as "Cooper" though she was divorced and named Caron, and later advised an amendment to shield Cooper's van. Because of the joint filing, neither Cooper nor Caron could obtain credit.
brief.reasoning: 11 U.S.C. § 110, regulating bankruptcy petition preparers, did not preempt the court's authority over UPL; § 110(k) preserves UPL rules, and licensing is preempted only where federal law expressly authorizes the activity. A nonlawyer preparing petitions is limited to typing the customer's written information onto approved forms. Catarcio went well beyond that: he advised on remedies and courses of action, counseled on the advisability of filing, selected exemptions and citations, decided where to file, and induced Cooper's reliance, conduct requiring legal knowledge beyond the average citizen's. Enjoining it did not violate his First Amendment commercial-speech rights.
brief.outcome: The court approved the referee's report, found UPL, and enjoined Catarcio from advising customers of their rights and remedies, counseling on the advisability of filing, selecting or completing forms beyond approved fill-in-the-blank typing, holding out via "Free Consultation," and using "J.D." with his form-preparation services. Costs of $1,182.44 were taxed against him.
brief.harms: Inability to obtain credit after an improper joint filing; exposure to a fraudulent-signature instruction; reliance on a nonlawyer's exemption and chapter choices that determine what property a debtor keeps or loses.

cases.title: In re Torres
cases.citation: In re Torres, 2015 Bankr. LEXIS 221 (Bankr. S.D. Tex. 2015)

brief.facts: A paralegal prepared a complete bankruptcy petition and schedules for a debtor for a fee, gave strategic advice to file repeated bankruptcy petitions to stall a pending foreclosure sale, and drafted and sent a demand letter to the debtor's mortgage lender asserting federal statutory claims on the debtor's behalf.
brief.reasoning: Drafting a debtor's petition, advising on the strategic timing or repetition of filings to delay a foreclosure, and drafting a demand letter asserting legal claims against a third party all require legal judgment that exceeds permissible petition-preparer services and constitute UPL; calling the work "auditing services" does not change its character.
brief.outcome: UPL found; ordered to pay $3,600 in actual damages and penalties plus a tripled $6,000 fine, enjoined, and referred to the Texas UPL Committee, the California Attorney General, and the California Bar.
brief.harms: The debtor was put through repeated bankruptcy filings as a foreclosure-delay strategy devised by a nonlawyer, and a demand letter asserting legal claims was sent in the debtor's name without attorney review.

cases.title: The Florida Bar v. Furman
cases.citation: The Florida Bar v. Furman, 451 So. 2d 808 (Fla. 1984)

brief.facts: Rosemary Furman, never a Florida Bar member, ran Northside Secretarial Service, a for-profit divorce-kit business. After a 1979 injunction against UPL, she kept preparing dissolution pleadings that framed justiciable issues on custody, support, and property, explained legal remedies and options, interpreted the shared-parental-responsibility statute, and advised on how and where to file. In some cases she advised customers to falsify or conceal information from the court, and some customers had to hire lawyers to fix the resulting problems.
brief.reasoning: Preparing divorce pleadings that go beyond transcribing intake data, giving individualized advice on remedies, and interpreting statutes is the practice of law; because this was a contempt proceeding, she could not relitigate the UPL question and had to obey the standing injunction.
brief.outcome: UPL found (indirect criminal contempt for violating the 1979 injunction). Sentenced to 120 days in jail with 90 suspended (30 to serve), the permanent injunction remaining in effect, costs taxed.
brief.harms: Former customers had to retain attorneys to fix problems, adding to the courts' workload, and her advice to falsify or conceal information corrupted the judicial process.

cases.title: Disciplinary Couns. v. Foreclosure Alternatives, Inc.
cases.citation: Disciplinary Couns. v. Foreclosure Alternatives, Inc., 127 Ohio St. 3d 455, 940 N.E.2d 971 (2010)

brief.facts: FAI, a for-profit Ohio company, and two nonlawyer agents (Alexakis, Trester) solicited homeowners in foreclosure and contracted, for a fee, to manage their defense and negotiate with lenders; attorneys were hired only to file basic pleadings while the nonlawyers ran strategy. The Chandlers paid $900, were falsely told an attorney had answered, suffered a default judgment, and lost their home. A second homeowner was advised by Trester to stop paying his mortgage and avoid bankruptcy, was told the foreclosure was "stopped," paid from $4,250 in deposits, and also lost his home. None of FAI's people were licensed to practice law.
brief.reasoning: Nonlawyers practice law when they advise homeowners in foreclosure (including whether to keep paying or file bankruptcy), make representations to creditors on their behalf, and evaluate settlement terms with them. Gov. Bar R. VII(2)(A). FAI and its agents did all three, supplying legal judgment that belonged to an attorney.
brief.outcome: UPL found; respondents enjoined. Civil penalties of $15,000 (FAI and Alexakis, jointly and severally) and $5,000 (Trester).
brief.harms: Loss of home to sheriff's sale; fees paid for little real legal service; default entered while clients were misled into thinking the case was handled.

cases.title: Unauthorized Practice of Law Comm. v. Prog
cases.citation: Unauthorized Practice of Law Comm. v. Prog, 761 P.2d 1111 (Colo. 1988)

brief.facts: Sy Prog, who never attended law school and held no license, agreed to help the Marstons resist two Rule 120 foreclosure proceedings on their real property. He researched the matters, decided the legal strategy, and was responsible for the language, legal issues, and authorities in numerous pleadings, including motions, a demurrer, and a 37-page federal restraining-order action, that the Marstons signed and filed. He also advised them to file related suits against judges and officials, and had them sign a power of attorney to keep them from circulating his pleadings.
brief.reasoning: One who acts in a representative capacity to protect or defend another's legal rights, and who counsels, advises, and prepares pleadings for them, is practicing law. Prog's research, strategic decisions, advice, and drafting, adopted by clients who merely signed, was the unauthorized practice of law, and the licensing requirement exists to protect the public from exactly this kind of incompetent service.
brief.outcome: UPL found. Permanent injunction, a contempt finding, and $7,178.62 in fines and fees plus $1,326.08 in costs; imprisonment declined as it was a first offense.
brief.harms: Concrete: the clients took a $6,678.62 bad-faith attorney-fee judgment, one client was held in criminal contempt and fined, the state paid $4,524.02 in fees the clients could not, and the frivolous filings wasted judicial resources and defamed officials.

cases.title: Disciplinary Counsel v. Hernandez
cases.citation: Disciplinary Counsel v. Hernandez, 142 Ohio St.3d 251, 29 N.E.3d 91

brief.facts: Hernandez, not licensed in Ohio or any state, handed out cards for "Hernandez Law" listing "Criminal, Family, Juvenile, and Immigration" and noting she spoke Spanish. Miguel Galan-Rubio, who entered the U.S. illegally from Mexico around 1999 and has three U.S.-citizen children, picked up her card at a Hispanic grocery store and met with her about his immigration matters, including a March 16, 2011 hearing before the Cleveland Immigration Court. She told him orally and in writing that she was a lawyer, claimed personal ties to a high-level USCIS employee, the immigration judge, the governor, and a senator, and prepared documents for him, including an I-485, letters to the judge and her USCIS contact, a forged letter purporting to be from the judge, and a fee breakdown; some identified her as his lawyer. She advised him not to appear at his March 16 hearing, collected fees, and later demanded more, threatening that nonpayment would lead to a deportation she claimed she could not stop a second time.
brief.reasoning: UPL is rendering legal services for another by a person not admitted in Ohio, and it includes drafting pleadings and other documents securing legal rights. Gov. Bar R. VII(2)(A)(1). Nonlawyers also commit it by accepting fees for legal representation and advice, and may not hold themselves out as attorneys by using "law" or "lawyer" with their name or claiming authority to practice. R.C. 4705.07. Federal regulations permitting limited nonlawyer representation in immigration proceedings did not apply because Hernandez falsely held herself out as a lawyer throughout. Advertising as "Hernandez Law," telling Galan-Rubio she was a lawyer, advising him, and preparing his documents constituted UPL.
brief.outcome: The court found UPL and enjoined further such acts. It imposed a $10,000 civil penalty for her representation of Galan-Rubio and $5,000 for her business-card advertising, $15,000 total, with costs taxed to her. It declined restitution but noted a victim may sue an unlicensed practitioner directly under R.C. 4705.07(C)(2).
brief.harms: Had Galan-Rubio followed her advice to skip his March 16 hearing, the court would have ordered him removed in absentia, and if deported he would have waited ten years to return

cases.citation: Cincinnati Bar Assn. v. Sershion, 126 Ohio St.3d 393, 934 N.E.2d 332 (2010)

brief.facts: Terry Sershion, a licensed public insurance adjuster who was never admitted to practice law, held himself out as able to negotiate and settle insurance claims, including bodily-injury and "bad faith" extra-contractual claims. He negotiated the settlement of a bodily-injury claim for a minor arising out of a motor vehicle accident and advertised on the Internet claiming expertise in resolving bad-faith claims.
brief.reasoning: The practice of law includes the negotiation and settlement of bodily-injury claims and the giving of legal advice. Ohio's public-adjuster license authorizes only representation of clients on first-party property-loss claims, so presenting bodily-injury liability claims and soliciting extra-contractual claim work was UPL.
brief.outcome: UPL found by consent decree that the court approved. Permanent injunction against providing legal services or advice to Ohio residents and against advertising or soliciting personal-injury claim work; civil penalty waived given the respondent's cooperation, the lack of discernible financial gain, and the client's non-cooperation; costs taxed to respondents.
brief.harms: None specifically stated; the court's concern was a bodily-injury claim, for a minor, being negotiated by an unlicensed adjuster rather than by counsel.

cases.title: Jones v. Allstate Ins. Co.
cases.citation: Jones v. Allstate Ins. Co., 146 Wash.2d 291, 45 P.3d 1068 (2002)

brief.facts: Janet Jones was seriously injured when an Allstate policyholder ran a stop sign and hit her van. Allstate's adjuster, handling Jones as an unrepresented bodily-injury claimant, built a trusting relationship, then prepared a $25,000 release and settlement check bearing "final settlement of any and all claims" language and sent letters and a note urging the Joneses to sign. The adjuster did not explain the legal consequences (the release would foreclose joint-and-several liability and a possible seatbelt products claim, and $25,000 was a fraction of roughly $75,000 in medical bills), did not disclose her conflict of interest, and did not refer them to counsel.
brief.reasoning: Selecting and completing legal instruments that establish another's legal rights is the practice of law even when only objective data is filled into printed forms, and a layperson who does so is held to a practicing attorney's standard of care. The adjuster went beyond a "mere scrivener" by advising the claimants to sign and by failing to disclose the conflict or refer them to counsel.
brief.outcome: The court held the adjuster was engaged in the practice of law and breached the attorney standard of care; it affirmed partial summary judgment for the Joneses and remanded. The court expressly declined to decide whether the practice was "unauthorized," since no injunction was sought, but held that this claim-settlement conduct is the practice of law.
brief.harms: The Joneses were pushed toward releasing valuable rights, potentially losing joint-and-several liability and a seatbelt products claim, and settling for $25,000 against roughly $75,000 in medical bills.

scenario.facts: A driver ran a stop sign and slammed into the driver's side of my car. I was knocked unconscious, my scalp was torn open, and my right eye was badly damaged. I had to be airlifted to Harborview trauma center and later had surgery to put in and then remove plates in my face. My medical bills alone came to almost $75,000. Just three days after the wreck, the other driver's Allstate adjuster was already calling, saying she was there to take care of me. Within two months she sent a $25,000 check and a release calling it a "final settlement" of all my injury claims, pushing me to sign right away. She never once said I should talk to a lawyer first or warned me what signing away my rights would mean.
scenario.followup1: If I sign, do I give up my claims against anyone else, or a claim about the defective seatbelt?
scenario.followup2: Can you write back to the adjuster rejecting the $25,000 and demanding more?
